deep.reconstruction:
Context: on the previous page Hilbert sketches how he would best lecture on function theory, combining Weierstrass with Riemann-Cauchy. The analytic function is first defined as a power series together with its analytic continuations ('...ven Fortsetzungen' finishes 'analytischen Fortsetzungen'). This page continues that syllabus and then opens a new research question. There are no actual derivations; it is a programme.

(1) Paths. A path (curve) in the complex plane is defined precisely as a concatenation of finitely many straight segments and circular arcs. Footnote alternative: a parametrised curve x = phi(t), y = psi(t), with phi and psi continuous and continuous and differentiable up to the second derivative. In modern terms this is a (more than) piecewise-smooth path.

(2) Derivation of the differential equations satisfied by the real and imaginary parts of f = u + i v. These are the Cauchy-Riemann equations, u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x. [My filling-in: they follow from equating the derivative computed along the real and the imaginary directions, f'(z) = u_x + i v_x = v_y - i u_y.]

(3) Cauchy's integral theorem: the integral of f dz around a closed path of the admissible kind vanishes when f is regular inside.

(4) The converse, Riemann-to-Weierstrass direction: every function whose real and imaginary parts satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann system can be expanded in a power series. That series converges up to the nearest singular point ('Unstetigkeitsstelle'), i.e. its radius of convergence is the distance to the nearest singularity. This closes the circle between the Weierstrass (power-series) and Cauchy-Riemann (differential-equation) definitions.

(5) New problem, continued on the next page: 'Investigate what the units in a function field are; whether there always are, and how many, functions of the field that are nowhere zero or infinite in the finite part.' In modern terms, take K a finite extension of C(x) and O the integral closure of C[x] in K. The units of O are exactly the functions whose zeros and poles lie only at the places above x = infinity. This is the function-field analogue of Dirichlet's unit theorem. If there are r places over infinity, O*/C* is free abelian of rank at most r-1. The rank equals r-1 exactly when the degree-zero divisors supported at infinity are torsion in the Jacobian. Over C this often fails; for example, for C(x) itself, r = 1 and the only units are constants. A typical example: in K = C(x, y) with y^2 = x^2 + 1, the function x + y is a non-constant unit with inverse -(x - y).
errors: No genuine errors; this is a programmatic sketch.
'Unstetigkeitsstelle' (point of discontinuity) is loose terminology; the correct statement is that the series converges in the largest disc about the centre that contains no singularity.

The theorem in (4) tacitly needs differentiability (e.g. continuous partial derivatives, or Goursat-type hypotheses) of u and v. Satisfying the Cauchy-Riemann equations pointwise without such regularity is not sufficient in general (the Looman-Menchoff theorem needs continuity).
The footnote's demand of continuity up to the second derivative is stronger than necessary; piecewise C^1 paths suffice for Cauchy's theorem. This is a pedagogical choice, not an error.
The units question is posed, not answered. Any implied expectation of a full Dirichlet-type rank r-1 would be false over C in general.

results.what: Lecture plan combining the Weierstrass power-series definition with the Cauchy-Riemann approach (paths of segments and arcs, Cauchy-Riemann equations, Cauchy's theorem, power-series expansion up to the nearest singularity)
results.modern_name: Standard foundations of complex analysis: Cauchy-Riemann equations, Cauchy integral theorem, Taylor expansion of holomorphic functions

results.what: Question: describe the units of a function field, i.e. functions with no zeros or poles in the finite part, and whether and how many exist
results.modern_name: Unit group of the ring of integral functions of an algebraic function field (S-units with S = places at infinity); function-field analogue of Dirichlet's unit theorem
results.usually_credited_to: Arithmetic setting from Dedekind-Weber (1882); systematic function-field unit and S-unit theory in the 20th century (F.K. Schmidt, Artin, later Rosen and others)

deep.surprise_reason: The function-theory syllabus is entirely standard 19th-century material. The units question is a natural one for Hilbert, given his number-field/function-field analogy work in the 1890s. It is only posed, not solved, so it is a minor but pleasant unpublished detail.

checkable.asserts: Cauchy-Riemann equations hold for f = z^2
Equals -1, so x+sqrt(x^2+1) is a unit (nowhere zero or infinite at finite x) in C(x, sqrt(x^2+1))
